title: "Precision Medicine: Why All of Us Exists, and Where Our Classes Fit"
description: "What precision medicine means, why the All of Us Research Program was built for it, how each course series connects to the program's goals, and what our results can and can't say about individual people"
---

*All of Us* was created for **precision medicine**. This page explains what that means, and how each series in this course connects to it. It's a good starting point for any class, and a good closing discussion for every series.

## What is precision medicine?

Most medical advice is based on the **average** person in a study: the same screening age, the same first drug, the same advice for everyone. **Precision medicine** tailors prevention, diagnosis, and treatment to the **individual**, by taking into account how people differ in their genes, environment, and way of life.

The program's founding paper describes its purpose like this:

> *"The All of Us data repository should permit researchers to take into account individual differences in lifestyle, socioeconomic factors, environment, and biologic characteristics in order to advance precision diagnosis, prevention, and treatment."*
> — The All of Us Research Program Investigators, *New England Journal of Medicine*, 2019 ([doi:10.1056/NEJMsr1809937](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMsr1809937))

The program began in 2015 as the **Precision Medicine Initiative** cohort program. You'll still see the old name, *PMI*, in the survey data (class [5.1](surveys/5-1-survey-basics.qmd)).

## Why precision medicine needed a program like *All of Us*

The founding paper names three problems with earlier studies: they were **too small**, they **lacked diversity**, and they didn't collect **enough kinds of data** about each person. *All of Us* was designed to fix all three:

| Earlier studies | *All of Us* | Why it matters for precision medicine |
|---|---|---|
| Thousands to hundreds of thousands of people | A goal of **1 million or more** | Differences between people are often small; finding them needs very large numbers |
| Mostly people of European ancestry | A focus on groups **underrepresented in biomedical research**: by 2019, **80%** of participants with biospecimens were from these groups | A treatment or risk score built on one group may not work as well for others |
| One or two kinds of data | Health records, surveys, physical measurements, **genomes**, RNA and proteins, and **wearables**, for the same people | "Genes, environment, and lifestyle" can only be studied together if they're measured on the same people |
| Data downloaded project by project | One cloud workbench, open to any approved researcher | More researchers, and more questions, from the same data |

## How our series connect to the program's goals

The founding paper lists the program's **scientific goals**. Our series, all on the same type 2 diabetes question, touch most of them:

| Program goal (from the founding paper) | Where you practise it | What it looks like in our classes |
|---|---|---|
| **Discover genetic and environmental correlates with disease** | [Omics](omics/index.qmd) 4.1–4.4; [Surveys](surveys/index.qmd) 5.2–5.3 | A genetic risk variant (rs7903146 in *TCF7L2*); family history, smoking, income, education, and food security |
| **Discover disease biomarkers** | [Omics](omics/index.qmd) 4.5–4.7 | Genes and blood proteins that differ in type 2 diabetes, and which of them are genetically controlled |
| **Connect mobile health, digital health, and sensor data with clinical outcomes** | [Wearables](wearables/index.qmd) 6.1–6.3 | Daily steps, sleep, and heart rate measured **before** a diagnosis, then followed forward to new type 2 diabetes |
| **Improve understanding of health disparities** | [Surveys](surveys/index.qmd) 5.3; [Core](core/index.qmd) 3.1–3.2; [Omics](omics/index.qmd) 4.1–4.2 | Diabetes by income, education, and insurance; differences between groups in Table One; genetic ancestry |
| **Enable machine-learning applications** | Machine learning series (7.x, planned) | Predicting **who** will develop type 2 diabetes, from data collected before diagnosis |
| Develop new disease classifications; improve predictions of therapeutic safety and efficacy; support clinical trials | Not covered yet | Ideas for future classes, e.g. medication response (pharmacogenomics) |

The [Core series](core/index.qmd) underpins all of them: finding the right people (cohorts), cleaning and joining their data, and the models every later class uses.

## What our results can, and can't, say about one person

Precision medicine is about **individuals**. Almost every result in our classes is about **groups**. Keeping the two apart is the most important lesson of this page.

| Our classes find… | Which means… | It does **not** mean… |
|---|---|---|
| An odds ratio of about **1.25** per copy of rs7903146's T allele (class [4.2](omics/4-2-gwas-plink.qmd)) | On average, each copy goes with about 25% higher **odds** of type 2 diabetes | That a person with the allele will get diabetes, or one without it won't. One common variant changes an individual's risk only a little |
| People with type 2 diabetes more often had low household incomes (class [5.3](surveys/5-3-social-factors.qmd)) | A pattern across **groups** | That income causes diabetes, or that it tells you about a single person |
| People who walked more had lower rates of new diabetes (class [6.2](wearables/6-2-steps-and-t2d.qmd)) | An **association**, in a design that reduces reverse causation | That walking more will prevent diabetes **for you**: that needs a trial |

The founding paper is candid about these limits too:

- **"Association does not necessarily translate into causation."** It points to methods such as **Mendelian randomization** and **polygenic risk scores** as ways to learn more, and to clinical trials to test it.
- **The sample isn't random.** The program "was not designed with a formal statistical sampling method", so some results don't describe the US population (class [5.1](surveys/5-1-survey-basics.qmd): no survey weights).
- **Health records are messy.** EHR data "can be fragmented, incomplete, and inaccurate" (class [2.1](core/2-1-clean.qmd), and the case definition in the shared cohort query).

### From group results to individual care

Getting from our kind of result to precision medicine takes several steps, and each one is an active research area:

1. **Combine many factors.** One variant, or one survey answer, predicts little. **Polygenic risk scores** add up thousands of variants; **prediction models** combine genes, records, surveys, and wearables (our planned machine learning series).
2. **Check it works for everyone.** Today's polygenic risk scores are several times more accurate in people of European ancestry than in other groups, because most genetic studies so far were in people of European ancestry. Using them in clinics could **widen** health disparities (Martin et al., *Nature Genetics*, 2019, [doi:10.1038/s41588-019-0379-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41588-019-0379-x)). This is exactly the gap *All of Us*'s diversity is meant to close.
3. **Show cause, not just association**, with designs such as Mendelian randomization and, finally, clinical trials.
4. **Show it helps patients**: that tailoring care on the new information leads to better health than usual care.

## 💬 Discussion questions

Use these at the end of any series.

- **Which kind of data** in this series (genes, records, surveys, wearables) would you most want for **your** risk of type 2 diabetes? Why?
- **Who is missing?** Which groups are still underrepresented in our cohort (for example, people with no health records, or no smartphone for a wearable)? How could that affect a prediction made for them?
- **Group vs individual:** pick one result from the series. What would you need to know before telling a patient it applies to **them**?
- **Harm:** how could a precision medicine tool built on these data make care **less** fair? (The Research Use Statement asks about this too: see [Research Use Statement](../workspace/research-use-statement.qmd).)
